Everyday life · 24 November 2026

Teenage sleep is not laziness

Why teenagers find it hard to fall asleep early and get up early, and what can help at home.

"There's no getting them to bed" and "there's no getting them up" are two complaints heard in many homes with teenagers. It is not just unwillingness: the body changes at this stage.

A clock that shifts later

With puberty, the internal clock shifts later: melatonin, the hormone that prepares the body for sleep, starts being released later in the evening. In addition, sleep pressure, the need for sleep that builds up during the day, rises more slowly. The result is that many teenagers find it hard to fall asleep before eleven or midnight, even when tired.

How much sleep they need

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours for young people aged 13 to 18. Many sleep much less on weekdays and then try to catch up at the weekend, which pushes their clock even later and makes Monday harder.

Why it matters

Short sleep in teenagers is associated with worse school performance, more irritability, more symptoms of anxiety and depression, and greater risk of accidents. That is why several paediatric societies have recommended that secondary school classes should not start too early.

What can help

  • Keeping similar schedules every day, including weekends, without big differences.
  • Getting natural light in the morning and reducing bright lights and screens in the last hour before bed.
  • Leaving phones out of the bedroom at night, as a rule for the whole family, not as a punishment.
  • Avoiding caffeine and energy drinks in the afternoon.

If, despite all this, there is intense daytime sleepiness, loud snoring or insomnia that does not improve, it is worth talking to the family doctor or paediatrician.

References

  1. Carskadon, M. A. (2011). Sleep in adolescents: the perfect storm. Pediatric Clinics of North America, 58(3), 637–647.
  2. Paruthi, S. et al. (2016). Recommended amount of sleep for pediatric populations: a consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 12(6), 785–786.
  3. American Academy of Pediatrics (2014). School start times for adolescents. Pediatrics, 134(3), 642–649.
